report.source_text: On the evening of admission, the patient developed an acute feeling of illness, worsening nausea and vomiting, vertigo, perioral and left-hand numbness, and light-headedness. The primary team called the neurology team, stating that she had worsening mental status and had become more somnolent. She was then transferred to the intensive care unit (ICU) for neuro checks every hour. A CT angiogram was ordered and showed stable findings compared to the morning. Her neurologic exam at this time was significant for disorientation where she was confused as to where she was, bradyphrenia, moderate-severe dysarthria with trouble remembering words and muffled speech, left-sided ptosis, and bilateral mild ataxia with finger-nose-finger. She was started on a heparin drip, as it was suspected that propagation of the BAO was the cause of her deterioration. She was nil per mouth for the next three to four hours.

clinician.trajectory_summary: An 83-year-old woman with a history of atrial fibrillation (AF) and recent cessation of rivaroxaban presented with acute neurological symptoms including nausea, dry mouth, left-sided tingling, difficulty speaking, and mild dysarthria. An initial CT head was normal (E003). A CT angiogram (CTA) of the head and neck revealed an occlusion of the distal basilar artery with a cerebral perfusion deficit of the right superior cerebellar artery (E004). Initial neurological exam showed mild dysarthria (NIHSS 1) (E001). An MRI of the brain initially showed no acute infarcts or ischemia (E006). On the evening of admission, the patient's neurological status acutely worsened with new symptoms including worsening mental status, somnolence, moderate-severe dysarthria, and ataxia (E007). A mechanical thrombectomy was performed within an hour of these new symptoms (E008). The patient's condition significantly improved by the next morning, returning almost to baseline with no neurological deficits except mild dizziness (E009). A subsequent CTA showed a widely patent basilar artery (E010). An MRI on hospital day 3 showed diffusion restriction in the bilateral cerebellar hemispheres and central midbrain (E011). The patient was eventually discharged a few days later with resolved symptoms (E012).
